clue.text: Reformation in the air — it came without E Napier, for example

indicators.note: re-formation means forming the letters of the phrase afresh in a new order, once the E is set aside

parts.note: the single letter E that the clue says to leave out

explanation.surface: A historical musing on the Reformation, as if it arrived in the air, with a mention of the Scottish thinker Napier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformation' looks like the Protestant Reformation but signals rearranging: the letters of IN THE AIR IT CAME, 'without' one E, rearrange to the answer. John Napier was the Scottish inventor of logarithms.
explanation.definitionFit: John Napier, who devised logarithms, is a classic example of a mathematician who works with numbers.

clue.text: Put a gum on the guide called George

parts.note: an automatic is a self-loading gun
a pilot guides ships or planes

explanation.surface: An order to arm a tour guide whose name happens to be George.
explanation.walkthrough: RAF slang named the autopilot 'George', so 'called George' defines it. 'on' just places one piece above the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Airmen nicknamed the device that steers a plane by itself George.

clue.text: Parliament taken aback when I go over long tale of woe

indicators.note: taken aback means read backwards, so the parliament's name is turned round

parts.note: the Dail is the lower house of the Irish parliament

explanation.surface: A parliament is startled when someone recites a long sad story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken aback' reverses the Irish parliament, and 'I go over' puts I on top in this down answer. An 'Iliad of woes' is a long series of troubles.
explanation.definitionFit: Homer's epic of the Trojan War is long and full of sorrow, giving the phrase an Iliad of woes.

clue.text: Wheeler's route-guides

parts.note: a wheeler here is a cyclist, and what guides the route is the steering bar, not a map

explanation.walkthrough: 'route-guides' suggests maps or signposts; what steers a bicycle is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A cyclist steers with this bar, so it guides the way the bike goes.

clue.text: Instalment has one so gripped in deep confusion

indicators.note: gripped in means the letters are held inside the other part
confusion means the letters of deep are muddled into a new order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: One part of a serial in which someone is held in a deep muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confusion' turns DEEP into EPDE, and I plus SO are 'gripped in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A single part of a serialised story or broadcast is one episode.

clue.text: Bad name for a house of this type

definitions.text: for a house of this type
definitions.meaning: a house of ill repute is a brothel, in the old phrase a house of this kind

explanation.definitionFit: Notoriety is a poor reputation, and a brothel was once called a house of ill fame.

clue.text: Holly — the Italian's late wife

parts.note: il is the Italian for the
an ex is a former spouse

explanation.surface: A tree is linked to a dead Italian woman's husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' here means former, not dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Ilex is the botanical genus name of the holly tree.

clue.text: Horse-doctor lay in wretched state — tight!

indicators.note: in a wretched state means the letters are in a mess and need rearranging

parts.note: gee-gee is a child's word for a horse, written GG

explanation.surface: A vet lies about in a terrible condition and drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: GG, DR and LAY IN are all rearranged together 'in wretched state'. 'tight' means drunk on the surface but defines a miser.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight person is stingy with money, which is what a mean, ungenerous person is.

clue.text: In Lent, perhaps, it upset Letty North at times

parts.note: Lent is the name of a university term at Cambridge, so it exemplifies a term

indicators.note: upset means the letters are knocked over and set in a new order

explanation.surface: During Lent, someone named Letty is upset by something while north.
explanation.walkthrough: Lent term is the spring term at Cambridge. 'upset' rearranges LETTY and N (North) into TENTLY after IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something now and then, with gaps, is doing it on and off.

clue.text: Case about extended opening in pub lasting three years

indicators.note: in places the opening letter and the turned pub inside the word for a court case

parts.note: a case heard in court is a trial

indicators.note: the opening of the word extended is its first letter
about tells us to turn the word for a pub round, reading it backwards

parts.note: an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: A court case concerning a pub's application for extended opening hours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' turns INN into NNI; E (the opening of 'extended') plus NNI go 'in' TRIAL. 'Extended opening' reads as late licensing hours, which is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Something triennial happens every third year or lasts for a three-year period.

clue.text: Noble Bruce sometimes gets a game

definitions.text: Noble Bruce sometimes gets a game

parts.words: Noble Bruce sometimes gets a game
parts.note: the peer in question was Thomas Bruce, the earl who brought the Parthenon marbles to London, and his title is also the name of a Scottish town whose football club gets fixtures

explanation.surface: Someone called Bruce, a nobleman, is sometimes picked for a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Bruce, seventh Earl of Elgin, took the Parthenon sculptures to Britain; Elgin is also a town in Moray, Scotland, with a football club, Elgin City.
explanation.definitionFit: The earl's family name was Bruce, so his title stands for a noble of that surname.

clue.text: Stanley's pattern of current brass-bat

parts.note: Major-General Stanley in Gilbert and Sullivan's Pirates of Penzance sings that he is the very pattern of a modern Major-General, a brass-hat being a senior officer

explanation.surface: Someone named Stanley sets the pattern for today's top army officers.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Pirates of Penzance, Major-General Stanley sings 'I am the very model of a modern Major-General'; 'current' stands for modern and 'brass-hat' for a general.
explanation.definitionFit: A pattern to be copied is an exemplar, the sense of the song's famous line.

clue.text: Go back in the morning for these old characters

indicators.note: back tells us to read the word Go in reverse order

parts.note: a.m. stands for the morning hours

explanation.surface: Go back early in the day to look at some ancient inscriptions.
explanation.walkthrough: Ogam (also ogham) is the ancient Irish alphabet carved on standing stones; 'characters' means letters, not people.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogam is an early Celtic script, so its letters are ancient written symbols.

clue.text: She featured in a strip cartoon, naturally

definitions.text: She featured in a strip cartoon, naturally

parts.words: She featured in a strip cartoon, naturally
parts.note: a strip cartoon is a comic strip, but strip also hints at undressing, and naturally hints at being nude

explanation.surface: A woman who of course appeared in a comic strip.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mirror's wartime comic strip heroine Jane was famous for losing her clothes; 'strip' and 'naturally' (as in naturism) carry the double meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mirror strip's heroine, a pin-up who kept ending up undressed, bore this name.

clue.text: Attacks women vulgarly over side-issue

indicators.note: over places the women on top of the next piece in this down answer

parts.note: broads is vulgar American slang for women

indicators.note: issue here means the letters of side come out in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone insults women crudely over a minor point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'issue' rearranges SIDE into IDES, under BROADS.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is a fierce verbal or naval bombardment, an assault.

clue.text: Protective cap does not prevent the limb being broken

indicators.note: being broken tells us the letters of the limb are smashed and put back together differently

explanation.surface: A protective cap fails to stop someone's arm or leg being broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being broken' signals rearranging THE LIMB. The cap is the one worn on a sewing finger.
explanation.definitionFit: A sewer wears this small metal cover on a fingertip to guard against the needle.

clue.text: Meeting envisaged about introduction of tugs on East River

indicators.note: about means the outer phrase goes around the inner letters

parts.note: something envisaged is in view, in sight

indicators.note: the introduction of tugs is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A meeting is planned concerning the arrival of tugboats on the East River in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: IN VIEW goes 'about' T, E and R. The East River is real, which hides E and R as two separate abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal face-to-face session for questioning someone is a meeting.

clue.text: Real trouble with party member of high rank

indicators.note: trouble suggests the word Real is thrown into disorder and rearranged

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party
M is an abbreviation for member, as in MP

explanation.surface: Genuine trouble involving a party member in a senior position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member of high rank' reads as one phrase; split it so 'high rank' defines and 'member' gives M.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of an earl is one of the higher grades of the British peerage.

clue.text: He provides vehicle to carry new tree

indicators.note: to carry means the vehicle holds the other letters within it

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of tree are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A man supplies a truck to transport a freshly bought tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He provides' looks like the start of a sentence but defines a trade; 'to carry' puts the rearranged tree inside the vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A person in this trade supplies food and drink for functions, so he provides.

clue.text: Prepares to publish what the Russians have done

parts.note: Reds was a common name for Soviet Russians, singular Red
acts are things done, deeds

explanation.surface: Something that prepares to print what the Soviet Union did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'what the Russians have done' reads as Red acts.
explanation.definitionFit: To redact is to edit text into shape for publication.

clue.text: Freudian consultant said to be compiler of records -

indicators.note: said to be signals that a word is spoken, and what we hear matches the answer

parts.note: an annalist writes yearly records or annals

explanation.surface: A psychoanalyst is reputedly someone who keeps records.
explanation.walkthrough: ANNALIST, a writer of annals, sounds like the answer. The trailing dots lead into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A psychoanalyst trained in Freud's methods is commonly called by this shorter title.

clue.text: Measure of the pressure variation round Darien

indicators.note: variation means the letters are varied into another order

parts.note: O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A gauge recording the change in pressure around Darien in Panama.
explanation.walkthrough: O and DARIEN are rearranged by 'variation'. Darien is the region of Panama.
explanation.definitionFit: An aneroid barometer measures air pressure without using liquid.

clue.text: …relating to what certain reactions reveal

definitions.meaning: a Latin-derived phrase meaning concerning or on the subject of
split re-actions and the start of the word reads as ..., so these reactions literally contain RE

explanation.walkthrough: The dots join this clue to the previous one in the surface only. A reaction, written with a hyphen as re-action, has RE in it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase is used in letters and law to mean concerning or on the matter of.

clue.text: The advantage, for example, of French backing

indicators.note: backing means the whole run of letters is read from right to left

parts.note: de is the French word for of

explanation.surface: An example of French financial backing gives an advantage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns the whole run of both pieces round, not just the French word.
explanation.definitionFit: To have the edge over someone is to have a slight lead or superiority.

clue.text: Mournful — that's Miss Thompson

parts.note: sad means mournful
i.e. is short for id est, that is

explanation.surface: A gloomy woman introduced as Miss Thompson.
explanation.walkthrough: Sadie Thompson is the prostitute in Somerset Maugham's story Rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Maugham's story Rain features a woman named Sadie Thompson, filmed several times.

clue.text: Couple get very little time in cathedral

parts.note: a duo is a pair
a mo is a moment, a very short time

explanation.surface: A pair get a moment in a cathedral.
explanation.walkthrough: Duomo is the Italian word for a cathedral, as in Florence or Milan.
explanation.definitionFit: Italians call the main church of a city its duomo.

clue.text: Mars land-measures

definitions.meaning: Mars is the Roman god of war, matched by his Greek counterpart
units of area of a hundred square metres each

explanation.definitionFit: The Greek war god corresponds to Roman Mars, and an are is a metric unit of area.

clue.text: Cockney draper got out of bed?

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: a hosier sells stockings and socks, a kind of draper

explanation.surface: A London draper who has got up in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Osiers are willow rods cut from an osier bed, so 'got out of bed' is their source, not a person rising.
explanation.definitionFit: Willow shoots for basketry are grown in beds and harvested from them.

clue.text: Excludes, for lack of space, many new words not in fashion

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, a crossword convention for many

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of words are given a fresh order

parts.note: out means no longer fashionable

explanation.surface: Lots of newly coined words that are unfashionable get left out because there is no room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'many' gives C, the Roman hundred; 'new' rearranges WORDS into ROWDS.
explanation.definitionFit: When a crowd pushes others away because there is no room, it shuts them out.

clue.text: Part of New York's Conservative -good show!

parts.note: the West Side is a district of Manhattan, with the s from the possessive
a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A British Conservative visiting a district of New York shouts his approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'New York's' supplies the S. 'good show!' sounds like British praise, but defines a good musical show.
explanation.definitionFit: Bernstein's Broadway musical is a celebrated stage show, hence a good one.
